summary: Comments from Vint Cerf that review and expand on the mail transition plan. It discusses how to keep mail, the most heavily used network service, working while moving from ARPANET protocols to Internet protocols, with the least disruption to users and software.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 773 discusses how to keep mail working while the ARPANET moves from NCP-based to TCP-based operation. It describes explicit and implicit forwarders for hosts with different levels of support for the transition.

questions: how did rfc 773 propose transitioning mail to tcp
subtitle: Comments on keeping mail working during a transition from NCP to TCP.

tldr.problem: Mail must continue to work while hosts using old NCP mail and new TCP mail coexist, with limited changes to users and programs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo distinguishes explicit forwarding by hosts with new tables from implicit forwarding for old NCP hosts that cannot identify TCP-only destinations.
tldr.outcome: It expands on a transition plan and lists remaining design tasks, including how to maintain mailbox registrations at implicit forwarders.

today: RFC 773 is a 1980 memo reviewing and expanding a mail transition plan. Its proposed schedule says the transition to TCP mail would be complete by January 1, 1983.

sections.title: Transition Goals
sections.content:
The memo reviews a plan for supporting electronic mail during the transition from ARPANET protocols to Internet protocols. It aims to preserve ARPANET mailbox names, avoid changing mail header parsers, accommodate non-ARPANET names, forward mail automatically, and keep old mail mechanisms working during the transition.

This memo addresses the first step, transition from NCP-based text mail to TCP-based text mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail should continue to work while hosts move to new protocols. Users and mail programs should need as few changes as possible.

sections.title: Explicit and Implicit Forwarding
sections.content:
A host with new Internet tables can identify whether a destination supports NCP or TCP and explicitly select a forwarder when the protocols differ. A host still using old NCP tables cannot identify that a destination is TCP-only.

For that case, the memo proposes an implicit forwarder: an old NCP host maps an Internet host name to a forwarding host, and TCP-only mailbox names are registered there so the forwarder can determine the final destination.
sections.plainLanguage: A host that knows about both protocols can choose a forwarder directly. An unchanged NCP host needs a forwarding host that already knows where registered TCP mailboxes belong.

sections.title: Host Types and Forwarder Requirements
sections.content:
The memo considers three cases: unchanged old NCP mail, NCP mail with new Internet tables, and TCP mail with new tables. It describes direct delivery or forwarding for pairs of these host types, with implicit forwarding required for old NCP to new TCP.

Forwarders must support both NCP and TCP. The memo assigns mail service to socket or port 57 and describes old FTP mail arriving at socket 3 at implicit forwarders.
sections.plainLanguage: The three kinds of hosts have different ways to exchange mail. The forwarding host must understand both NCP and TCP to relay between them.

sections.title: Open Work and Proposed Schedule
sections.content:
The memo lists unresolved work on error reporting, choosing forwarding hosts, collecting and distributing Internet mailbox names, distributing host capability tables, and handling mail systems that are incompatible with NCP, TCP, or RFC 733.

It proposes dates for introducing forwarding and ending the transition, but presents these as a schedule to encourage the transition.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo leaves several operational details to be worked out, including forwarder selection and mailbox registration. It also gives a proposed schedule for ending the transition services.
